concepts.title: Lift
concepts.hook: A paper glider has no engine, yet its wing can hold it up while air moves past. When it slows, that upward force fades.
concepts.rule: A wing makes lift when air flows past it and is turned down. The air pushes the wing up. Lift grows with speed squared, and in steady level flight it equals weight.

claims.text: Lift needs air moving past a wing. No air or no motion means no lift.
A wing turns the air that flows past it, and the air pushes back on the wing. That push is lift.
The idea that air over the top must meet the air below at the back edge is wrong. Flat wings lift too.
Lift grows with the square of the speed, so twice the speed gives four times the lift.
In steady cruise, a plane's lift equals its weight.

items.stem: On a still school sports day, Arjun holds his paper glider in the air and lets go without throwing it. What will it do?

options.text: It drops, since no air flows past.
options.feedback: With no throw and no wind, no air moves past the wings, so there is no lift.

options.text: It hovers, since its shape lifts.
options.feedback: Shape alone makes no lift. Air has to flow past the wings first.
Nothing pushes it up. Without moving air, the glider simply falls.

items.stem: Isha says a wing would lift even better on the Moon, where there is no air to slow it. What is she missing?

options.text: With no air, there is nothing to make lift.
options.feedback: Lift comes from turning air. On the airless Moon, a wing makes no lift.

options.text: The Moon pulls things down harder.
options.feedback: The Moon's pull is weaker than Earth's. The real problem is that it has no air.
A wing needs air to turn. Where there is no air, there is no lift.

items.stem: Which of these can make lift?

options.text: A kite held still in a steady wind.
options.feedback: The kite is still, but the wind moves past it. Moving air is what counts.

options.text: A wing resting in a still, closed room.
options.feedback: Nothing moves past this wing, so it makes no lift.

options.text: A wing spinning in empty space.
options.feedback: Empty space has no air, so the wing has nothing to turn.

items.stem: Put these in order for how a wing gets lift.

options.text: Air flows over the tilted wing.
options.feedback: First the air has to reach the wing and flow past it.

options.text: The wing bends that air downward.
options.feedback: Next the tilted wing turns the moving air down.

options.text: The air pushes back on the wing, upward.
options.feedback: Last, the turned air pushes the wing up. That push is lift.

items.stem: Why can a flat paper wing, the same shape on top and bottom, still lift?

options.text: It turns air down when it is tilted.
options.feedback: Lift comes from turning air. A tilted flat wing does that, so it lifts.

options.text: Air on top races to catch up.
options.feedback: That equal-time idea is wrong. A flat wing lifts because it turns air.
Paper is much heavier than air. It lifts by turning the air down.

items.stem: On a train, Om puts his flat palm out of the window and tips the front edge up. What does he feel?

options.text: His hand is pushed up and back.
options.feedback: His palm turns air down, so it is pushed up. The air also drags it back.
Tipping the front edge up turns air down, which pushes the hand up.

options.text: Nothing, since a palm is flat.
options.feedback: Flat surfaces still turn air when tilted, so his hand gets pushed.

items.stem: A wing makes 100 newtons of lift at one speed. About how much lift does it make at twice that speed, all else the same?

options.feedback: Lift grows with speed squared. Two times two is four, so 100 becomes about 400.
That doubles the lift. Lift grows with speed squared, so it is about four times.
More speed gives more lift. Twice the speed gives about four times as much.

items.stem: A plane cruises level at a steady speed. Its lift equals its ___.

options.feedback: In steady level flight, lift holds up the weight, so the two are equal.
In cruise, thrust balances drag. Lift is what balances the weight.
That is not a force at all. In steady cruise, lift equals the weight.

misconceptions.name: Shape alone lifts
misconceptions.correction: A still wing needs moving air to make lift.

misconceptions.name: Air is not pushed
misconceptions.correction: Wings turn air; the air pushes back on them.

misconceptions.name: Equal time on top
misconceptions.correction: Air on top does not have to meet the air below. Flat wings lift too.

misconceptions.name: Lift keeps pace with speed
misconceptions.correction: Lift grows with speed times speed, so double speed gives four times the lift.

steps.title: Lift needs moving air

hook.stem: A kite lies flat on the grass on a still day. What does it need before it can rise?

options.feedback: Right. A kite or wing only lifts when air flows past it.
Shape matters, but with no moving air even a light kite makes no lift.
Sunshine does not lift a kite. It needs air flowing past it.

steps.teach: A wing only lifts when air flows past it. Move the wing, or let wind blow over it. No air or no motion means no lift.

example.ask: Tap what makes the lift.
parts: Riya runs across the school ground,
so air rushes over her paper glider's wings,
and it floats up out of her hand.
example.spot: so air rushes over her paper glider's wings,
example.feedback: Air moving over the wings makes the lift. Without that flow, the glider just drops.

guided.stem: A model wing sits in a box with all the air pumped out. Someone shakes it. Does it lift?
guided.hint: Lift needs air to push on.

options.feedback: Right. With no air to turn, the wing makes no lift at all.
Speed alone is not enough. With no air, nothing gets turned, so no lift.
A wing needs moving air. In empty space it makes no lift.

guided.stem: A plane sits parked in calm air with its engines off. How much lift do its wings make?
guided.hint: Is any air flowing past the wings?

options.feedback: Yes. With no air moving past, the wings make almost no lift.
Lift needs moving air. A parked plane in calm air has almost none.
Nothing is flowing past the wings, so they make almost no lift.

steps.takeaway: No moving air, no lift.

steps.title: A wing turns air down, and the air pushes it up

hook.stem: Your hand is out of a bus window, tipped up a little. Where does the air go after it hits your palm?

options.text: Down, and your hand gets pushed up.
options.feedback: Right. Your hand turns the air down, so the air pushes your hand up.

options.text: Up, and it pulls your hand up.
options.feedback: The tipped hand sends air down, not up. The push back on your hand is upward.
The air is turned, not just slowed. Turning it down pushes your hand up.

steps.teach: A tilted wing bends the passing air downward. Push air one way and it pushes back the other way. That push back on the wing is lift.

example.ask: Tap the push that lifts the kite.
parts: A kite tilts into the wind,
it bends the air downward,
and the air shoves the kite upward.
example.spot: and the air shoves the kite upward.
example.feedback: The kite turns air down, so the air pushes the kite up. That upward push is lift.

guided.stem: A wing is set to turn air upward instead of down. Which way does the force on the wing point?
guided.hint: The force points the other way from the turned air.

options.feedback: Right. Turn air up and the air pushes the wing down.
The push on the wing is opposite to the turned air, so it points down.
Turning air always makes a push back, here pointing down.

guided.stem: Asha says the top of a wing is longer, so air on top must race to meet the air below. Is she right?
guided.hint: Think of flat paper wings that still fly.

options.feedback: Right. Flat wings with equal sides still lift, so that idea is wrong.

options.text: Yes, that is why wings lift.
options.feedback: NASA calls this idea wrong. Flat wings with equal sides lift too.

options.text: Yes, but only for big planes.
options.feedback: The idea is wrong for every wing. Wings lift by turning air.

steps.takeaway: A wing turns air down; the air pushes the wing up.

steps.title: More speed gives much more lift

hook.stem: A glider doubles its speed. Guess how its lift changes.

options.feedback: Right. Lift grows with speed times speed, so double speed gives four times.
Lift grows faster than speed. Double speed gives about four times the lift.
Faster air past the wing means more lift, about four times here.

steps.teach: Lift grows with speed times speed. Twice the speed gives four times the lift. So a plane must go fast before its wings can carry its weight.

example.ask: Tap the cause of the bigger lift.
parts: A jet rolls slowly down the runway,
then it reaches twice that speed,
and its wings now make four times the lift.
example.spot: then it reaches twice that speed,
example.feedback: Doubling the speed is the cause. Lift grows with speed squared, so it becomes four times bigger.

guided.stem: A plane flies at three times its slowest speed. How much more lift can its wings make, all else equal?
guided.hint: Multiply the speed change by itself.

options.feedback: Right. Three times three is nine, so lift grows ninefold.
Lift grows with speed squared, so triple speed gives nine times.
Square the speed change: three times three is nine, not six.

guided.stem: A plane cruises level at a steady speed. How does its lift compare with its weight?
guided.hint: Steady and level means the forces balance.

options.feedback: Right. In steady cruise, lift and weight are equal.
Extra lift would make it climb. In steady cruise, lift equals weight.

options.text: Lift is much less than weight.
options.feedback: Then it would sink. In steady cruise, lift equals weight.

steps.takeaway: Double the speed, four times the lift.

concepts.title: How a multirotor turns
concepts.hook: A quadcopter can spin in place while its four rotors stay flat. It does this by changing how hard each pair of rotors twists.
concepts.rule: A multirotor changes motor speeds to shift thrust. Uneven thrust tilts it in pitch or roll, and the tilt moves it. A change in the balance of the spin pairs turns it in yaw.

claims.text: A thrust gap between opposite rotors tilts a drone in pitch or roll.
Yaw comes from a thrust gap between the two pairs of rotors that spin opposite ways.
Two rotors spin clockwise and two spin the other way, so their twists on the body cancel.
In a hover, each of the four rotors carries about a quarter of the weight.
A drone moves sideways by tilting, which points part of its total thrust that way.

items.stem: A drone that weighs 20 newtons hovers on four rotors. About how much thrust does each rotor give?

options.feedback: In a hover, each rotor carries a quarter of the weight. 20 divided by 4 is 5.
That is the whole weight. Four rotors share it, so each gives about 5.
That multiplies by four. The rotors share the weight, about 5 newtons each.

items.stem: At a school fair, a hovering drone has a small bag hung under it. To keep hovering at the same height, what must its rotors do?

options.text: All speed up to add thrust.
options.feedback: More weight needs more total thrust. Speeding all four keeps it level.

options.text: Nothing, since hovering costs no extra push.
options.feedback: Extra weight needs extra thrust, or the drone will sink.

options.text: Only the front two speed up.
options.feedback: That would tip the nose up. All four need to speed up together.

items.stem: To climb straight up without tilting, a drone speeds up ___ of its rotors.

options.feedback: Equal extra thrust on every rotor lifts it straight up and keeps it level.
Speeding just the front would tip the nose up, not lift it straight.
One pair alone would change the twist balance and turn the drone.

items.stem: In a college lab, a breeze pushes a hovering drone to the right. To push back to the left, how must it tilt?

options.text: Lean left, with its right rotors pushing harder.
options.feedback: The right side rises, the drone leans left, and its thrust now pushes it left.

options.text: Lean right, with its left rotors pushing harder.
options.feedback: Leaning right would push it further right, the same way as the breeze.

options.text: Stay level and turn its nose.
options.feedback: Turning the nose does not push it sideways. It needs to tilt left.

items.stem: Why does a drone that tips its nose down also start to fly forward?

options.text: Its thrust now points partly forward.
options.feedback: Tilting aims part of the rotor thrust ahead, so the drone speeds forward.

options.text: The front rotors pull it along.
options.feedback: Front rotors push up, not ahead. The tilt aims some thrust forward.
Gravity pulls straight down. Forward motion comes from tilted thrust.

items.stem: Match each drone motion with the rotor change that makes it.

options.feedback: A roll comes from one side pushing harder than the other.
The left side rises, so the drone rolls to the right.
A nose-down tilt comes from front and back thrust being uneven.
The back rises above the front, so the nose dips down.

items.stem: Dev says a drone turns its nose by leaning into the turn, like a bike. What is wrong?

options.text: It turns by unbalancing its two spin pairs.
options.feedback: Speeding one spin pair over the other twists the body, so the nose turns.

options.text: Drones cannot turn their nose at all.
options.feedback: They can. Unbalancing the two spin pairs turns the nose on the spot.

options.text: It turns by switching off one rotor.
options.feedback: That would drop it. It turns by unbalancing the two spin pairs.

items.stem: Which line best explains why a hovering drone does not spin on its own?

options.text: Its two spin pairs cancel each other's twist.
options.feedback: Two rotors spin each way, so their twists on the body cancel out.

options.text: Its GPS holds the nose still.
options.feedback: GPS gives position. The cancelling spin pairs stop the twist.

options.text: Its rotors spin too fast to twist it.
options.feedback: Fast rotors twist the body more. Opposite pairs are what cancel it.

misconceptions.name: GPS steers motors
misconceptions.correction: GPS can aid position, but speed changes at the motors make the turn.

misconceptions.name: All speeds same for turn
misconceptions.correction: A turn needs a change in the balance of motor forces.

misconceptions.name: Drones bank to turn
misconceptions.correction: A drone turns its nose by changing the twist balance, not by tilting.

misconceptions.name: Tilt is only for balance
misconceptions.correction: Tilting points thrust sideways, which is how a drone moves.

steps.title: Four rotors share the weight

hook.stem: A drone that weighs 2 newtons hovers on four equal rotors. How hard does each rotor push up?

options.feedback: Right. Four rotors share 2 newtons, so each gives about half a newton.
That is the whole weight. Split four ways, each rotor gives 0.5 newtons.
That is four times too much. The rotors share the weight, about 0.5 each.

steps.teach: To hover, the four rotors together push up as hard as the drone weighs. Each one carries about a quarter. Speed them all up and it climbs.

example.ask: Tap what makes the drone climb.
parts: The drone hovers over the cricket pitch,
then all four rotors speed up together,
and it rises straight up.
example.spot: then all four rotors speed up together,
example.feedback: Speeding all four rotors equally lifts total thrust above the weight, so it climbs without tilting.

guided.stem: A drone that weighs 12 newtons hovers on four rotors. What thrust does each rotor give?
guided.hint: Split the weight four ways.

options.feedback: Right. 12 divided by 4 is 3 newtons each.
That is the total. Each of the four rotors carries a quarter, 3 newtons.
That multiplies instead of dividing. Each rotor gives 3 newtons.

guided.stem: All four rotors slow down by the same amount. What does a hovering drone do?
guided.hint: Total push drops below the weight.

options.feedback: Right. Less total thrust than weight means it moves down, still level.
Tipping needs uneven thrust. Equal slowing just makes it sink.
Spinning needs the spin pairs unbalanced. Equal slowing makes it sink.

steps.takeaway: In a hover, four rotors share the weight equally.

steps.title: Uneven thrust tilts the drone, and the tilt moves it

hook.stem: The two back rotors of a drone push harder than the front two. What does it do first?

options.feedback: Right. The back rises, so the nose dips.
The harder-pushing back end rises, so the nose goes down, not up.
Spinning comes from the spin pairs. Front and back thrust tilts it.

steps.teach: Push harder on one side and that side rises, so the drone tilts. A tilted drone aims part of its push sideways, and it starts to move.

example.ask: Tap the cause of the tilt.
parts: At a college drone race, a quad leans left
because its right rotors push harder,
and then it slides to the left.
example.spot: because its right rotors push harder,
example.feedback: Extra thrust on the right lifts that side, so the drone rolls left and slides that way.

guided.stem: A drone needs to roll to its right. Which rotors should push harder?
guided.hint: The side that pushes harder rises.

options.feedback: Right. The left side rises, so the drone tips to the right.
That lifts the right side, which tips the drone to the left.
Equal thrust keeps it level. A roll needs one side to push harder.

guided.stem: A drone tilts forward and keeps its total push the same. Where does part of that push now point?
guided.hint: Thrust points along the tilted rotors.

options.feedback: Right. The tilt aims part of the thrust forward, so the drone moves ahead.
Rotor thrust points away from the rotors, up and now a bit forward.
Tilting changes where the push points. Part of it now points forward.

steps.takeaway: Uneven thrust tilts it; the tilt sends it sideways.

steps.title: Opposite spins let it turn on the spot

hook.stem: Why do two of a drone's rotors spin clockwise and two the other way?

options.text: So their twists on the body cancel.
options.feedback: Right. Each rotor twists the body; opposite pairs cancel out.
It is not about speed. Opposite spins stop the body from twisting.
Spacing keeps blades apart. Opposite spins cancel the twist on the body.

steps.teach: Each spinning rotor twists the body the other way. Two spin clockwise and two the other way, so the twists cancel. Speed up one pair and the drone turns.

example.ask: Tap why the drone turns.
parts: A hovering drone keeps its height,
but its clockwise pair spins a bit faster,
so its nose swings around.
example.spot: but its clockwise pair spins a bit faster,
example.feedback: The faster pair twists the body more than the other pair, so the drone turns its nose.

guided.stem: All four rotors on a test drone spin the same way. What happens to its body?
guided.hint: Nothing cancels the twist.

options.text: It keeps turning the other way.
options.feedback: Right. With no opposite pair, the twist is never cancelled, so the body spins.
Four twists in the same direction add up, so the body turns.
The twist is about the up-down line, so the body spins, not flips.

guided.stem: To turn, a drone speeds up one pair and slows the other. Why slow one pair at all?
guided.hint: Think about the total push.

options.text: To keep total thrust equal to weight.
options.feedback: Right. Faster here and slower there keeps the height steady while it turns.
The main reason is height. Slowing one pair keeps total thrust equal to weight.
Tilt comes from front and back thrust. Here the aim is steady height.

steps.takeaway: Spin pairs cancel twists; unbalance them to turn.

concepts.title: Batteries and flight time
concepts.hook: Doubling a drone battery does not double flight time. The bigger battery is heavier, so the motors work harder.
concepts.rule: Flight time is battery energy divided by the power used. More battery adds energy and weight, and hover power rises faster than weight, so flight time peaks and then falls.

claims.text: Flight time depends on stored energy and the rate at which it is used.
A heavy battery adds weight, so the craft needs more lift.
In the hover model, power grows as thrust to the power 1.5, so it climbs faster than weight.
Flight time rises with battery size only up to a peak, when the battery is about two thirds of the drone's mass. Past that, more battery cuts time.
In the Berkeley test, flying batteries let the main drone hover 57 minutes instead of 12.

items.stem: A drone battery holds 50 watt-hours and the drone hovers at 200 watts. About how many minutes can it fly?

options.feedback: 50 divided by 200 is a quarter of an hour, which is 15 minutes.
Dividing 200 by 50 flips the sum. Energy over power is a quarter hour, 15 minutes.
Adding the numbers does not work. Divide energy by power to get 15 minutes.

items.stem: For a school project, Kabir has two drones with the same battery. Drone A hovers at 80 watts, drone B at 160 watts. Which flies longer?

options.text: Drone A, about twice as long.
options.feedback: Both hold the same energy, and A spends it half as fast, so it lasts twice as long.

options.text: Drone B, since it has more power.
options.feedback: Using more power empties the battery faster, so B lands first.

options.text: Both the same, since the batteries match.
options.feedback: Same energy, but B spends it twice as fast, so it lands sooner.

items.stem: Flight time in hours equals battery energy in watt-hours divided by the ___ in watts.

options.feedback: Energy divided by the rate it is spent gives the time it lasts.
Weight is in kilograms, not watts. The divisor is the power used.
Rotor count is not in watts. Divide the energy by the power used.

items.stem: A college team adds a camera that doubles its drone's weight but keeps the same battery. Predict the new hover time, in the simple model.

options.feedback: Twice the weight needs nearly three times the power, so the same energy lasts about a third as long.
Power rises faster than weight, nearly threefold, so time drops to about a third.
The battery is the same, but the heavier drone spends its energy much faster.

items.stem: Tara says a drone that is twice as heavy needs exactly twice the hover power. What is not quite right?

options.text: Power rises faster, nearer three times.
options.feedback: In the hover model, power grows as weight to the 1.5 power, so it is nearly three times.

options.text: Power does not change with weight.
options.feedback: More weight needs more thrust, which needs more power, not the same.
A heavier drone needs more power to hover, not less.

items.stem: Same drone, same battery. Which load gives the shortest flight?

options.feedback: The heaviest load needs the most thrust and power, so the energy runs out first.
A light parcel adds little weight, so the flight stays longer than with 500 grams.
Carrying nothing needs the least power, so this gives the longest flight.

items.stem: Why does flight time fall once the battery is more than about two thirds of a drone's mass?

options.text: The extra weight costs more power than its energy adds.
options.feedback: Past the peak, each added gram of battery raises hover power more than it adds energy.

options.text: Big batteries hold less energy per cell.
options.feedback: The model keeps energy per kilogram fixed. The weight cost is what wins.

options.text: The motors get weaker with age.
options.feedback: Motor age is not the cause. Extra weight costs more power than it adds.

items.stem: Which line best sums up the Berkeley flying battery test?

options.text: Small drones bring fresh batteries, so the main drone avoids one huge battery.
options.feedback: Swapping batteries in flight beat the limit: 57 minutes of hover instead of 12.

options.text: One giant battery is always the best plan.
options.feedback: A giant battery passes the peak and shortens flight. Swapping smaller ones works better.

options.text: Flying batteries make the motors stronger.
options.feedback: The motors stay the same. The idea is to swap in fresh energy without extra weight.

misconceptions.name: Double size, double time
misconceptions.correction: More battery adds weight, so time need not scale with size.

misconceptions.name: Weight costs nothing
misconceptions.correction: More weight needs more lift and motor work.

misconceptions.name: Power keeps pace with weight
misconceptions.correction: Hover power rises faster than weight, so twice the weight needs nearly three times the power.

steps.title: Flight time is energy divided by power

hook.stem: A drone battery stores 50 watt-hours and the drone hovers at 100 watts. How long can it hover?

options.feedback: Right. 50 divided by 100 is half an hour.
That flips the sum. 50 watt-hours at 100 watts lasts half an hour.
Divide energy by power: 50 by 100 gives half an hour, about 30 minutes.

steps.teach: A battery is a store of energy. Flight time is that energy divided by how fast the motors use it. Use power faster, and the time shrinks.

example.ask: Tap the rate of use.
parts: Meera's drone battery holds 60 watt-hours,
its motors draw 120 watts in a hover,
so it can hover for about half an hour.
example.spot: its motors draw 120 watts in a hover,
example.feedback: Watts tell how fast energy is used. 60 watt-hours at 120 watts lasts half an hour.

guided.stem: A drone uses 200 watts and its battery holds 100 watt-hours. How long can it hover?
guided.hint: Divide energy by power.

options.feedback: Right. 100 divided by 200 is half an hour.
That divides the wrong way. 100 by 200 gives half an hour.
Too long. 100 watt-hours at 200 watts lasts half an hour.

guided.stem: Two drones have the same battery. One uses power twice as fast. How do their times compare?
guided.hint: Same energy, faster use.

options.text: The faster user lasts half as long.
options.feedback: Right. The same energy spent twice as fast runs out in half the time.
Same energy, but one spends it faster, so it runs out sooner.

options.text: The faster user lasts twice as long.
options.feedback: Spending energy faster empties the battery sooner, not later.

steps.takeaway: Flight time is stored energy divided by power used.

steps.title: Extra weight costs even more power

hook.stem: A drone gets twice as heavy. Guess the power it needs to hover.

options.feedback: Right. Hover power climbs faster than weight, nearly three times here.
Power grows faster than weight. Twice the weight needs nearly three times.
More weight needs more thrust, and power climbs even faster than thrust.

steps.teach: Heavier drones need more thrust to hover. Power climbs faster than thrust, so twice the weight needs nearly three times the power.

example.ask: Tap the hidden extra cost.
parts: A delivery drone picks up a heavy parcel,
its rotors push harder to hold it up,
and its hover power rises even faster than its weight.
example.spot: and its hover power rises even faster than its weight.
example.feedback: The weight goes up, but hover power goes up faster still, so flight time drops sharply.

guided.stem: A drone's weight goes up four times. In the simple model, how much does hover power go up?
guided.hint: Power goes as weight to the 1.5 power: 4 times the square root of 4.

options.feedback: Right. 4 times 2 is 8, so power rises eightfold.
Power climbs faster than weight. Four times the weight needs about 8 times the power.
Too small. Four times the weight needs about 8 times the power.

guided.stem: A drone with the same battery carries a small stone. Why is its flight shorter?
guided.hint: Same energy, but what about power?

options.text: It needs more power to hover.
options.feedback: Right. More weight means more thrust and more power, so the energy runs out sooner.
The stone uses no power itself. Carrying it makes the motors work harder.

options.text: The battery now holds less energy.
options.feedback: The battery holds the same energy. It is spent faster on a heavier drone.

steps.takeaway: More weight needs more thrust, and power rises even faster.

steps.title: Bigger batteries hit a limit

hook.stem: Keep adding battery to a drone. What happens to its flight time?

options.text: It rises, then peaks, then falls.
options.feedback: Right. At first extra energy wins; later the extra weight costs more.
Extra battery adds weight, and past a point the weight wins, so time falls.
Small batteries gain a lot from more energy. Time rises before it peaks.

steps.teach: More battery adds energy but also weight. Flight time rises at first, then peaks when the battery is about two thirds of the mass. After that, more battery cuts time.

example.ask: Tap the peak.

steps.teach: When the Sun is low, its light crosses far more air to reach you. Along the way, most blue gets scattered out. Mostly reds and oranges are left.

example.ask: Tap why the Sun looks red.
parts: From a train window, Om watches the evening Sun,
its light crosses a long stretch of air,
and mostly reds and oranges get through.
example.spot: its light crosses a long stretch of air,
example.feedback: The long path through air scatters out the blue, so reds and oranges are left.

guided.stem: Smoke or dust fills the air at sunset. What can happen to the colours?
guided.hint: More bits in the air scatter away more short waves.

options.text: The sunset can look even redder.
options.feedback: Right. Pollution can scatter away even more of the shorter waves.
Extra particles strip out more blue, so the sunset gets redder.
Particles scatter more short waves, which can deepen the reds.

guided.stem: Which path through the air is longer: sunlight from a low Sun or from a high Sun?
guided.hint: Low light skims through the air.

options.feedback: Right. Light from near the horizon crosses much more air.
Overhead light takes the short path straight down through the air.
The low Sun's light slants through far more air.

steps.takeaway: A longer path through air scatters out blue, leaving red.

concepts.title: Pressure cooker
concepts.hook: A sealed cooker raises pressure, so water can boil at a higher temperature.
concepts.rule: Higher pressure raises water's boiling point. A sealed cooker reaches about 121°C, so food cooks faster. Its vent weight lets out steam to hold the pressure steady, and a safety device backs it up.

claims.text: Water boils at more heat when the air above it has more push.
A pressure cooker can cook faster because its hot liquid and steam reach above an open pot’s normal boil.
A typical cooker vents at about 15 pounds per square inch above air pressure, about double, so water boils near 121°C.
Air pressure is lower on hills, so water boils cooler: about 193°F, near 89°C, at 10,000 feet.
While water is boiling, its temperature stays the same.
Indian standard cookers use a free dead weight on the vent to hold the pressure, plus a separate safety device.
The Indian standard says to fill a cooker no more than two thirds full, or half full for foods that swell, like rice.

items.stem: On a hostel trek high in the hills, the group cooks rice in an open pot. Predict the cooking time compared with the plains.

options.text: Longer, since water boils cooler up there.
options.feedback: Lower air pressure up high lowers the boil, so food cooks more slowly.

options.text: Shorter, since the air is thinner.
options.feedback: Thin air lowers the boiling point, so cooking takes longer, not shorter.
The boil is cooler up high, so food takes longer to cook.

items.stem: Why does a big flame not make an open pot of boiling water any hotter?

options.text: Boiling water stays at one temperature; extra heat just makes more steam.
options.feedback: While water boils, its temperature holds steady. More flame only boils it off faster.

options.text: The flame is too far from the water.
options.feedback: The flame is close enough. Boiling water simply holds one temperature.

options.text: Water cools down as it boils.
options.feedback: It does not cool. Its temperature stays the same while it boils.

items.stem: On a high hill, lower air pressure makes water boil at a ___ temperature than at sea level.

options.feedback: Less air pressure lowers the boiling point, so water boils cooler up high.
A hotter boil needs more pressure, like in a cooker. Hills have less.
The boil depends on pressure, and hills have less, so it is lower.

items.stem: A cooker vents at about 15 psi above outside air pressure, which is about 14.7 psi. About what is the total pressure inside, in psi?

options.feedback: Add the 15 psi extra to the 14.7 psi outside to get about 30 psi, roughly double.
15 psi is only the extra. Add the 14.7 psi outside to get about 30.
That multiplies the numbers. Add them instead to get about 30 psi.

items.stem: For a school cooking club, Kavya cooks chana in a pressure cooker and Raj in an open pot, on the same flame. Whose chana softens first?

options.text: Kavya's, since her water boils hotter.
options.feedback: Her cooker raises the pressure, so the water boils near 121°C and cooks faster.
Escaping steam keeps an open pot at 100°C, so it cooks more slowly.

options.text: Both together, since both are boiling.
options.feedback: Boiling in a cooker is hotter, so Kavya's chana softens first.

items.stem: Sana says a cooker is faster because pressure squeezes flavour and heat into the food. What is not quite right?

options.text: Pressure raises the boiling point; hotter water cooks faster.
options.feedback: The extra pressure lets water boil near 121°C, and that heat cooks food faster.
Pressure works by raising the boiling point, not by squeezing.

options.text: Cookers are not faster at all.
options.feedback: They are faster, because their water boils hotter than an open pot.

items.stem: Put the steps of a cooker's whistle in order.

options.text: Steam builds and the pressure rises.
options.feedback: First, heating the sealed cooker makes steam, and the pressure climbs.

options.text: The pressure lifts the vent weight.
options.feedback: Next, at its set pressure, the steam pushes the weight up.

options.text: Steam escapes and the pressure stays steady.
options.feedback: Last, the escaping steam stops the pressure from climbing further.

items.stem: Kunal is cooking rice, which swells, in a pressure cooker. By the Indian standard, how full may the cooker be?

options.feedback: For foods that swell, like rice, the standard says to fill no more than half.
A full cooker is unsafe. For rice, fill it no more than half.

options.text: Up to two thirds, the general limit.
options.feedback: Two thirds is the limit for most food. Swelling foods like rice stop at half.

misconceptions.name: Pressure pushes flavour in
misconceptions.correction: The extra push lets the water boil at a higher heat.

misconceptions.name: More flame raises an open boil
misconceptions.correction: Boiling water stays at the same heat, however big the flame.

misconceptions.name: The whistle only says food is done
misconceptions.correction: The vent weight lets out steam to hold the pressure steady.

steps.title: The boiling point depends on pressure

hook.stem: Trekkers high on a mountain boil water for tea. Guess how hot the boiling water gets.

options.feedback: Right. Lower air pressure up high makes water boil below 100°C.
100°C is for sea level. Up high, water boils cooler.
That needs more pressure, as in a cooker. Up high it is less.

steps.teach: Water's boiling point depends on the air pressing on it. On hills, the air presses less, so water boils below 100°C. More pressure means a hotter boil.

example.ask: Tap why the dal cooks slowly.
parts: In a hill town, Tenzin boils dal in an open pot,
the thin air lets the water boil below 100°C,
so the dal takes longer to soften.
example.spot: the thin air lets the water boil below 100°C,
example.feedback: Lower air pressure on hills lowers the boiling point, so the cooler water cooks slowly.

guided.stem: At 10,000 feet, water boils at about 193°F. About what is that in Celsius?
guided.hint: It is about 11 degrees below 100°C.

options.feedback: Right. 193°F is close to 89°C.
100°C is the sea-level boil. Up high it is about 89°C.
That is the boil inside a pressure cooker. Up high it is about 89°C.

guided.stem: An open pot of water is boiling hard. You turn the flame up. What happens to the water's temperature?
guided.hint: Boiling water holds one temperature.

options.feedback: Right. While it boils, its temperature stays put; it just boils off faster.
An open pot cannot boil that hot. The temperature stays the same.
More flame does not cool it. The temperature stays the same.

steps.takeaway: Less pressure, cooler boil; more pressure, hotter boil.

steps.title: A sealed cooker boils hotter

hook.stem: A pressure cooker traps steam. About how hot can its boiling water get?

options.feedback: Right. At working pressure, water boils near 121°C.
That is an open pot. Trapped steam lifts the boil to about 121°C.
Too high. A home cooker boils water near 121°C.

steps.teach: A sealed cooker traps steam, so the pressure inside builds up. At about double the outside pressure, water boils near 121°C. Hotter water cooks food faster.

example.ask: Tap why the rajma cooks faster.
parts: Amma seals the rajma in the pressure cooker,
the trapped steam lets the water reach about 121°C,
so the beans soften in far less time.
example.spot: the trapped steam lets the water reach about 121°C,
example.feedback: Trapped steam raises the pressure, so the water gets hotter than 100°C and cooks faster.

guided.stem: Which is hotter: an open pot boiling on a big flame, or a cooker boiling on a low flame?
guided.hint: Pressure, not flame, sets the boil.

options.feedback: Right. Its higher pressure lets its water boil near 121°C.
A big flame cannot push an open boil past 100°C. The cooker is hotter.
The cooker's pressure makes its water hotter than the open pot.

guided.stem: Both pots are boiling. Why does food cook sooner in the cooker?
guided.hint: Compare the water temperatures.

options.feedback: Right. Hotter water cooks food faster.

options.text: Pressure pushes flavour into the food.
options.feedback: The real reason is heat: higher pressure means hotter boiling water.
Flame size does not set the boil. Pressure does.

steps.takeaway: Trapped steam raises pressure, so water boils near 121°C.

steps.title: The vent weight keeps the pressure steady

hook.stem: What does the weight on top of a cooker's vent do?

options.text: Lets out steam to keep the pressure steady.
options.feedback: Right. It lifts at its set pressure and lets steam out.

options.text: Locks in all the steam for good.
options.feedback: It does the opposite. It lifts and lets steam out at the set pressure.

options.text: Only shows when the food is done.
options.feedback: The whistle is a side effect. Its job is to hold pressure steady.

steps.teach: The weight on the vent lifts when pressure gets high and lets steam out, so pressure stays steady. A separate safety device opens if pressure climbs far too high.

example.ask: Tap what keeps the pressure steady.
parts: The cooker heats up on the stove,
the vent weight lifts and lets out a whistle of steam,
so the pressure inside holds steady.
example.spot: the vent weight lifts and lets out a whistle of steam,
example.feedback: When the weight lifts, extra steam escapes, so the pressure cannot keep climbing.

guided.stem: Why must the vent stay clear and never be covered?
guided.hint: Steam needs a way out.

options.text: So extra steam can escape and pressure stays safe.
options.feedback: Right. A clear vent lets the weight do its job.
A clear vent is about safety. It lets extra steam escape.
It is about safety, not looks. Steam must be able to escape.

guided.stem: Cooking is done, but the cooker is still under pressure. What is the safe step?
guided.hint: The lid is built to stay shut until pressure is low.

options.text: Wait until the pressure has fully dropped.
options.feedback: Right. Open the lid only once the pressure is gone.
Never force it. Wait until the pressure has fully dropped.

options.text: Shake the cooker to free the lid.
options.feedback: Shaking a hot cooker is risky. Wait for the pressure to drop.

steps.takeaway: The vent weight holds pressure steady; a safety device backs it up.
